newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Eurotunnel faces new Channel challenge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Eurotunnel faces new Channel challenge.

text.p: LONDON - Eurotunnel's multi-billion-pound debt restructuring deal will give the Anglo-French company an opportunity over the next few years to get itself into financial shape and thrive in the competitive cross-Channel market, analysts said on Monday.
But experts said it was premature to predict its long-term survival owing to the uncertainties of the transport market, and the heavy debt burden Eurotunnel still carries.

"They are sustainable now, they can keep the tunnel running, but the long wait before they start facing up to their debts makes it very, very difficult to value the company," said one transport analyst at a large investment bank in London.
"Unless you really believe Eurotunnel is going to grow massively over the next few years it is hard to see the long-term valuations stacking up," added the analyst, who asked not to be named.

The key point of the deal Eurotunnel has struck with the leaders of its banking syndicate is to trim its annual interest bill and even let it postpone payment of some of this interest during the next few years, at no additional cost.
The principal on its junior debt, which has been more than halved to 4.0 billion pounds ($6.26 billion), will not be addressed until 2004.
Therefore, analysts said, the deal meant Eurotunnel's financial future would become sustainable -- for a time -- but brought with it new risks linked to its future ability to pay.

The company estimated on Monday that its initial annual interest bill will be about 400 million pounds, and it has a war chest of up to 1.85 billion pounds of so-called stabilisation notes that it can use to settle any interest it cannot afford.

"If you look at the current cash flow of between 150 and 200 million pounds a year, what they can't find (to meet the 400 million interest bill) they will roll forward into the stabilisation notes, and they can keep that going for seven, eight or nine years," another analyst said.

Eurotunnel's outgoing British chairman, Sir Alastair Morton, said he saw some hope for a boost to operating profits if, as he expected, the current phase of deep fare discounting by both the tunnel and its rival ferry companies ends soon.

He told reporters on Monday he hoped a planned joint venture between ferry operators P&O of Britain and Sweden's Stena Line would go ahead and bring with it rationalisation of ship capacity on the all-important Dover-Calais route.
